passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after I have baptized her today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative singular participle agrees with Peter, the speaker. The English explicitly makes him the baptizer, not the children. Its event is within the rhetorical question’s contemplated action, not a statement that baptism has already occurred.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, interrupting the continuous grammatical connection with ἀπέλαβον τέκνα. The English reads the surviving words continuously as “from the time I have recovered my own children.” The supplied Greek and its printed punctuation are not changed; no missing wording is restored. This is a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not an assertion of OCR error or publication-blocking source corruption.

passages.text: “Since your mother approaches baptism with faith, let her fast at least one day before baptism.” But she swore, “For two of the days that have passed, while telling the woman about the recognition, I was unable to partake of food because of my great joy, except for a little water yesterday alone.” Peter’s wife testified to her oath, saying, “She has indeed tasted nothing.” Aquila—or rather, henceforth Faustinianus—said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” Peter laughed and answered, “But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Perhaps, then, God, wishing our mother not to be separated from the table for even one day after recognizing us, arranged the fast beforehand. For just as she remained chaste in ignorance, doing what accords with the truth, so perhaps God has now arranged for her to fast a day beforehand, in ignorance, for the sake of the true baptism, so that from the very first day of recognizing us she may partake of salt with us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it did not take place for that purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἤ literally introduces “or.” The main English “since it did not take place for that purpose” treats this as an explanatory reformulation: the earlier abstention is not a baptismal fast precisely because it was not undertaken for baptism. A more source-transparent explanatory disjunction is “But this is not a baptismal fast—or, rather, it did not take place for that purpose.” This preserves the printed disjunctive form while making the reformulation readable. “Unless it took place for that purpose” is only a contextual paraphrase of the criterion, not a direct alternative rendering of the printed ἢ μὴ clause and not a different Greek reading. No source correction is asserted.
The feminine day is understood from the surrounding fasting discussion; no longer duration is added.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let not evil overcome us by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext. Rather, let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today, and tomorrow she will be baptized. Indeed, the hour of today is not suitable for baptism.” And we all agreed together that it should be done this way.

lexical_decisions.rationale: This can be abstract badness or personified evil. The main text leaves the personification without explicitly naming a devil.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared exhortation and repeated reference to “you” are both retained in grammatical English. The text calls for holding out through the day; no new independent baptismal requirement is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρόφασιν εὑροῦσα τὴν πρόνοιαν καὶ τεκούσης στοργήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόνοια can mean care, concern, or forethought, as well as providence. Its pairing here with a mother’s affection supports ordinary care as the excuse Peter warns against; the source does not name whose care it is. “By finding a pretext in providence and a mother’s affection” remains a lexical alternative, particularly in light of Faustinus’s preceding proposal of divine arrangement. The main text does not uniquely impose divine governance as the meaning.

passages.text: “But perhaps someone will say, ‘How many have perished because of chastity?’ I say it was because of insensibility. For a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor, must immediately flee association with him as she would a blazing fire or a rabid dog. This is what your mother did, truly loving the beauty of chastity. Therefore she was preserved and received with us the knowledge of the eternal kingdom. A woman who wants to remain chaste must know that, envied by evil, she has many who plot against her under the pretext of love. Yet by the single resolve to remain chaste, continuing honorable and gaining victory over them all, she will be able to be saved. For the prophet said that, even if someone does every good thing, for the single sin of committing adultery one must be punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αἰσθανομένην ἢ γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text carries the perception expressed by αἰσθανομένην into the second alternative by ellipsis: “who finds” is not a second printed perception verb. γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ is a genitive absolute stating someone’s becoming a suitor. A viable alternative retains it as a circumstance of the required flight: “For the woman who becomes aware—or when someone has become a suitor—must immediately flee association with him.” The main text instead treats both alternatives as ways the danger becomes apparent, supported by the initial perception language and immediate call to flee. The printed ἤ is retained in both analyses. A smoother “who notices that someone has become a lover” suppresses that disjunction and is therefore only a paraphrase, not a direct rendering of this edition. ἐραστής can mean pursuing lover or suitor, not necessarily someone whose advances have been accepted.
The agent can be personified evil or human wickedness; no particular demon or person is supplied.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.
The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.
The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῖς κρείττοσιν as neuter, referring to better circumstances, supported by the recovery of the children after danger and separation. “Among better things” is a more literal neuter rendering but can obscure the situational sense. The same form permits a masculine interpretation, “among better people,” which would locate them with a better group, for example their present associates, rather than characterize their circumstances. Neither interpretation is uniquely established; the legitimate-origin wording is retained separately and no particular group is named.
